dossier.thesis: Backs very early-stage founders at high volume, about 100 new startups a year. He uses his media platforms (podcasts, events, newsletter) to find deals and help founders. In 2026 LAUNCH is leaning toward AI and agent startups.

Founders with lived experience in the problem
Solutions to painful problems that scale simply

brief.headline: Jason Calacanis backs very early-stage, high-agency founders at volume, and a fanbase-specific night-out layer on top of concert tickets is a clear, painful-problem pitch he can judge quickly at pre-seed or seed.
brief.angle: Open with the problem in one sentence: a concert ticket gets you into the show, but the night around it (bars, merch, rides) is left to chance. Then show how fast you've executed and why you personally understand the problem. If your per-fanbase picks are driven by AI or agents, say so plainly, since LAUNCH is leaning that way in 2026. If they aren't, don't force it.

name_drop.line: Our concertgoers show a 0.788 affinity with Robinhood, so they're used to opening an app and acting in the moment, which is the same behavior we need on show night.
name_drop.name: Robinhood

name_drop.line: Our audience has a 0.782 affinity with Thumbtack, so they're comfortable booking real-world services through an app, and we apply that to pre-show bars and rides.
name_drop.name: Thumbtack

name_drop.line: Calm has a 0.773 affinity with our crowd, which suggests they value an app that removes friction from their routine. We take the planning stress out of a night out.
name_drop.name: Calm

deck: Lead with the problem in one clear slide: the ticket is the easy part, and the night around it is fragmented and unplanned.
Show execution speed early: what you've built and shipped, and how quickly, so the high-agency signal is visible in the first few slides.
State your lived experience with the problem and why you're the one to solve it.
Use Ticketmaster, Spotify and Uber as comparables to show the simple scaling logic: ticket intent, fanbase taste, and rides or logistics combined into one flow.
Add a slide on the 25–29 core audience and how it differs from the 35–44 skew of his portfolio's crowd, framed as a new, reachable audience. Only use numbers you can back up.

openers.line: I've followed This Week in Startups, and your push for founders to explain the problem simply shaped how I built this pitch. Here's the problem in one sentence.
openers.name: This Week in Startups

openers.line: I saw you also launched The TWIML AI Podcast this year. We're thinking hard about how smart recommendations can personalize a night out for each fanbase.
openers.based_on: The TWIML AI Podcast (formerly This Week in Machine Learning & Artificial Intelligence)
openers.name: The TWIML AI Podcast (formerly This Week in Machine Learning & Artificial Intelligence)

openers.line: I'm a regular TechCrunch reader, and I'd like to show you the numbers behind how fans actually spend a show night.
openers.name: TechCrunch

avoid: Don't pitch a vague 'AI-powered' story. His 2026 lean is toward AI and agents, but he also wants a clear articulation of the problem, so only claim AI where it's real.
Don't bury the lede or ramble. He backs about 100 startups a year and values fast execution and clarity.
Don't present a big, abstract vision without proof of speed. Show what you've actually built and shipped.
questions: Why are you the right founder for this, and what lived experience do you have with the problem?
How fast have you moved, and what have you shipped or tested with real fans so far?
How does this scale simply across fanbases, venues and cities without heavy manual curation?
Where does AI or agent technology actually make your picks better for each fanbase?
Why would Ticketmaster or a ride app not just build this themselves?
